action: Scan every open-weight model when it is brought in, before it runs. Flag undisclosed merged fine-tunes, test flagged models for hidden triggers, and decide to block, quarantine or approve on evidence rather than the model card.
exec: Downloaded AI models are third-party code; a cheap hidden backdoor is feasible, though so far shown only in the lab.
plain: CrowdStrike showed in the lab that freely shared AI models can carry hidden instructions that only switch on with a secret trigger, and described a way to check models before using them.

key_findings: Organisations that download open-weight models they cannot verify are at risk, most of all where agents run tool calls automatically.
A backdoored fine-tune behaves normally until a keyword or date triggers it; a cited demonstration cost about $50 to build.
Three backdoor classes are described: agent, code and safety (refusal removal).
In a lab test of 16 models the pipeline flagged all 8 backdoored ones and recovered a trigger for each.
Fine-tuning can weaken a model's refusals as a side effect even in adapters built for unrelated tasks.
recommendations: Scan every open-weight model statically when it is ingested.
Escalate flagged models to trigger recovery, using the static findings to choose which behaviour to test.
Decide before deployment whether to block, quarantine or approve each model on evidence, not its model card.
Treat open-weight models like any other third-party code.

summary: CrowdStrike published lab research on AI models that behave normally until a trigger word or date makes them act maliciously, for example by calling an attacker's address. It cites a demonstration that cost about $50 to build. Its two-stage method, weight comparison then trigger recovery, flagged all eight backdoored models in a 16-model test. No real-world cases are reported.
title: CrowdStrike shows how to detect backdoors hidden in open-weight AI model fine-tunes

validation.note: Reviewed against the original CrowdStrike report.
